adjudication_label: batch_2:Anisotropic lattice strain and stress generation in oxides
canonical_question: How does the lattice contraction in the a-axis (0.26%) compare quantitatively to the c-axis contraction (0.76%) in the CrTaO4 phase, and what does this anisotropy imply for stress?

question_variants.question: How does the lattice contraction in the a-axis (0.26%) compare quantitatively to the c-axis contraction (0.76%) in the CrTaO4 phase, and what does this anisotropy imply for stress?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The a-axis contraction (0.26%) is approximately one-third of the c-axis contraction (0.76%). The provided text quantifies these values but does not explicitly state the physical implication of this anisotropy for stress; it only reports the lattice constants and percentage differences.

answers.answer: The lattice constants of the CrTaO4-based oxide detected after 200 hours were a = 4.630 Å and c = 2.997 Å. These values were 0.26% less in the a-axis and 0.76% less in the c-axis compared to pure CrTaO4. The text provides the quantitative comparison but does not explicitly interpret the stress implication of this anisotropy.
answers.mechanism: Anisotropic lattice contraction observed in oxide phase
answers.boundary_limitation: No explicit stress calculation or implication provided in the text
evidence_spans: isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours
The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3
At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours
